e.etymology: A clipped spelling of True, the English word for 'real, faithful', also heard as a short form of Truman and Truett.

assoc.t: Tru by Hilton, the budget hotel chain

e.etymology: From Latin augustus, 'majestic, venerable', the title the Roman Senate gave Octavian, the first emperor, in 27 BC. The month of August is named for him.
namesakes: Augustus (first Roman emperor)
Augustus Gloop (greedy boy of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory)
Augustus Waters (hero of The Fault in Our Stars)

assoc.t: Augustus Caesar, the first Roman emperor

e.etymology: From Greek Damon, from damazein, 'to tame, subdue'. In the classical story of Damon and Pythias, Damon stakes his life on his friend's return, which made the name a byword for loyal friendship.
namesakes: Damon Wayans (comedian and actor)
Damon Salvatore (vampire of The Vampire Diaries)

assoc.t: Matt Damon, the actor

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Charlie, the pet form of Charles and Charlotte, from Germanic karl, 'free man'. Pop star Charli XCX and TikTok's Charli D'Amelio made the spelling familiar.
namesakes: Charli XCX (pop star behind the album Brat)
Charli D'Amelio (TikTok star)

assoc.t: Charli XCX, pop star of the album Brat
Charli D'Amelio, TikTok star

e.etymology: The Spanish form of Stephen, from Latin Stephanus and Greek Stephanos, crown or wreath. Saint Stephen, the first Christian martyr, spread the name across Europe.
A Latinate feminine form of Carolus (Charles), from a Germanic word for a free man. North and South Carolina were named for King Charles I of England.
namesakes: Carolina Herrera (Venezuelan-American fashion designer)

assoc.t: North Carolina and South Carolina, US states
Carolina Panthers NFL team and Carolina Hurricanes NHL team

e.etymology: From Greek Matthias, a short form of Mattathias, from Hebrew Mattityahu, gift of Yahweh; the same source as Matthew. In the New Testament Matthias is the apostle chosen to replace Judas.
namesakes: Saint Matthias (apostle chosen to replace Judas Iscariot)

e.meaning: ivory, the creamy white material of tusks
e.etymology: As a modern given name it comes from the English word ivory. There is also an older surname Ivory, from Ivry in Normandy.

assoc.t: elephant-tusk material and the off-white color
Ivory soap, Procter & Gamble's white bar soap

e.etymology: An English spelling of Irish Ciarán, from Old Irish ciar, black or dark, with a diminutive ending. Several early Irish saints bore the name.
namesakes: Kieran Culkin (actor, Succession)

e.etymology: A modern American name with no settled derivation. It follows the sound of Zaria and Mariah and echoes the Biblical name Azariah.
From the English occupational surname for a chandler, someone who made or sold candles. The word came into English from Old French.
namesakes: Chandler Bing (Matthew Perry's character on Friends)

assoc.t: Chandler Bing, the wisecracking friend on Friends
Chandler, Arizona, a large Phoenix suburb

e.etymology: From an English surname that began as an Anglo-Norman nickname for an unlucky person, from Old French maleure, unhappy or unlucky. The 1980s sitcom Family Ties made it a popular girls' name.
namesakes: Mallory Keaton (the older daughter on the sitcom Family Ties)

e.etymology: A modern phonetic spelling of Michaela, the feminine form of Michael, from Hebrew for who is like God. It rose in the 1990s alongside Mikayla and McKayla.
A recent name of unknown derivation. It spread among Spanish-speaking American families after singer Larry Hernandez's daughter Daleyza appeared on the reality show Larrymania.
A modern spelling of Riley. Riley comes both from an English place name meaning rye clearing and from the Irish surname Reilly.
The Spanish and Portuguese form of Isaiah, through Latin and Greek from Hebrew Yeshayahu, Yahweh is salvation. Isaiah is one of the major prophets of the Bible.

assoc.t: Hurricane Isaias, which hit the US East Coast in 2020

e.etymology: From Hebrew Rafa'el, God has healed, through Greek and Latin. Raphael is one of the archangels and appears as a healer and guide in the Book of Tobit.
namesakes: Raphael (Italian Renaissance painter)
Raphael Warnock (US senator from Georgia)

assoc.t: Raphael, Italian Renaissance painter
Raphael, the red-masked Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtle

e.etymology: From the Lorelei, a steep rock on the Rhine whose name is read as murmuring rock or lurking rock. German legend puts a siren there who lured boatmen to their deaths. It is not used as a name in Germany.
namesakes: Lorelei Lee (Marilyn Monroe's showgirl in Gentlemen Prefer Blondes)

assoc.t: Lorelai Gilmore of Gilmore Girls (spelled Lorelai)
Lorelei rock on the Rhine and the siren of German legend

e.etymology: Isabella spelled with a z, the usual form in Hungarian. Isabella comes from Isabel, the medieval Spanish form of Elizabeth, Hebrew for my God is an oath.
The English form of Greek Dorothea, from doron, gift, and theos, god. In use since the 15th century, it was one of the top American girls' names of the 1920s.
namesakes: Dorothy Gale (heroine of The Wizard of Oz)
Dorothy Parker (writer and wit)
Dorothy Zbornak (Bea Arthur's character on The Golden Girls)

assoc.t: Dorothy Gale, the Kansas girl in The Wizard of Oz

e.etymology: From the English word destiny, used as a given name since the 1970s. The word comes through Old French from Latin destinare, to determine.

assoc.t: Destiny's Child, Beyonce's R&B group
Destiny, Bungie's sci-fi shooter video game series

e.etymology: A feminine form of Daniel, from Hebrew for God is my judge. It is a variant of Daniela and Danielle.
From the Japanese word ronin, a samurai without a master, taken up as an American boys' name from films and comics. Its closeness to the Irish name Ronan helped it along.

assoc.t: Japanese term for a samurai without a master
Ronin, 1998 Robert De Niro thriller, and 47 Ronin

e.note: In Japan ronin is a common noun, not a name; today it also means a student retaking college entrance exams.

e.meaning: the French capital; also the Trojan prince of Greek myth
e.etymology: As a modern name it usually honors the French capital, named for the Parisii, a Gaulish tribe. Paris is also the Trojan prince of Greek myth whose abduction of Helen began the Trojan War.
namesakes: Paris Hilton (hotel heiress and media personality)
Paris Jackson (model and daughter of Michael Jackson)
Paris of Troy (prince in Greek myth who carried off Helen)

assoc.t: Paris, the capital of France
Paris Hilton, heiress and reality TV star

e.meaning: descendant of the little fair one
e.etymology: From the Irish surname Ó Fionnagáin, descendant of Fionnagán, a pet form of Fionn, fair or white. James Joyce's novel Finnegans Wake carries the name.

assoc.t: Finnegans Wake, James Joyce novel and Irish ballad

e.etymology: From the Irish surname Ó Caiside, descendant of Caiside, a byname from cas, curly. It has been a popular American girls' name since the 1980s.

assoc.t: Butch Cassidy, Wild West outlaw

e.meaning: dweller; also a spelling of Beau, handsome
e.etymology: In the US mostly a spelling of Beau, French for handsome, or a short form of Beauregard. The Scandinavian name Bo comes from Old Norse Búi, dweller or long-time resident.
namesakes: Bo Jackson (two-sport NFL and MLB star)
Bo Burnham (comedian and filmmaker)
Bo Derek (actress, 10)

assoc.t: Bo Jackson, two-sport star of the Bo Knows ads
Bo, the Obama family's Portuguese water dog

e.etymology: From the Roman name Fabianus, belonging to Fabius, a clan name traditionally tied to Latin faba, bean. A 3rd-century pope and saint bore it, and the Normans brought it to England.
namesakes: Fabian (late-1950s teen idol singer Fabian Forte)

assoc.t: Fabian, late-1950s teen idol singer

e.etymology: The Italian word for white, a cognate of French Blanche. English speakers met it through Shakespeare, who used it in The Taming of the Shrew and Othello.
namesakes: Bianca Jagger (human rights advocate and 1970s style icon)

e.etymology: From a Norman surname taken from places in France called Quincy, ultimately from the Roman name Quintus, fifth. President John Quincy Adams made it familiar in America.
namesakes: Quincy Jones (music producer and composer)
John Quincy Adams (sixth US president)

assoc.t: Quincy Jones, music producer behind Thriller
Quincy, Massachusetts, city just south of Boston
Quincy, M.E., 1970s TV medical examiner

e.etymology: From the English word felicity and the Latin name Felicitas, good fortune, borne by early Christian martyrs including Saint Felicity of Rome.
namesakes: Felicity Huffman (actress, Desperate Housewives)
Felicity Jones (actress, Rogue One)

assoc.t: Felicity Merriman, American Girl's colonial-era doll
Felicity, late-1990s college drama with Keri Russell

e.etymology: A respelling of McKenna that appeared in the 1980s. McKenna is an Irish surname meaning son of Cionaodh, a Gaelic personal name.
